tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use the default 5-minute Anthropic prompt-cache TTL. Sleeping past 300 seconds means the next wake-up reads your full conversation context uncached — slower and more expensive. So the natural breakpoints:

- **Under 5 minutes (60s–270s)**: cache stays warm. Right for actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about — a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue.
- **5 minutes to 1 hour (300s–3600s)**: pay the cache miss. Right when there's no point checking sooner — waiting on something that takes minutes to change, genuinely idle, or as the long fallback heartbeat when something else is the primary wake signal.

**Don't pick 300s.** It's the worst-of-both: you pay the cache miss without amortizing it. If you're tempted to "wait 5 minutes," either drop to 270s (stay in cache) or commit to 1200s+ (one cache miss buys a much longer wait). Don't think in round-number minutes — think in cache windows.

For idle ticks with no specific signal to watch, default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop checks back, you don't burn cache 12× per hour for nothing, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Think about what you're actually waiting for, not just "how long should I sleep." If you're polling a CI run that takes ~8 minutes, sleeping 60s burns the cache 8 times before it finishes — sleep ~270s twice instead.

The runtime clamps to [60, 3600], so you don't need to clamp yourself.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
**Overall:** the design is strong and production-minded, often above typical best practice. The code style is the big weakness: much of it is written so densely that it will be hard for anyone to maintain. There are also a few places where the service builds its own version of something .NET already provides, or where a safety choice was taken too far.

## What it does well

**Messaging and data consistency**
- **Idempotent projection.** A unique `event_id`, a payload hash and a Duplicate/Conflict classification ([ProjectionStore.cs:50-52](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Persistence/ProjectionStore.cs#L50-L52)) make redelivered messages safe.
- **Acknowledges only after the database commit.** It even handles the case where it can't tell whether the commit succeeded: it re-reads the database before acknowledging ([ProjectionStore.cs:23-29](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Persistence/ProjectionStore.cs#L23-L29)). Most implementations skip this.
- **Bad messages are quarantined with publisher confirms before the original is acknowledged**, so a rejected event is never silently lost.
- **Reconnection** uses exponential backoff with jitter, and shutdown drains in-flight messages within the host timeout.

**Search reads**
- **Keyset (cursor) pagination, not OFFSET**, backed by matching composite indexes ([SearchDbContext.cs:40-41](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Persistence/SearchDbContext.cs#L40-L41)).
- **Signed cursors.** They use HMAC with key IDs so keys can be rotated, are tied to the original query, expire, and are checked with a constant-time comparison.
- **Stable pages.** Each cursor records a snapshot of the ingestion sequence, so new jobs arriving mid-scroll don't shift results between pages.
- **Safe LIKE matching.** User input is escaped (`%`, `_`, `\`), and trigram GIN indexes back the `ILIKE` searches.

**Configuration, operations and build**
- Every options class is validated with `ValidateOnStart`, and the database enforces constraints, timeouts and lock timeouts itself.
- Errors are returned as ProblemDetails with trace IDs; internal details are never leaked.
- Separate live, ready and ingestion health endpoints.
- `TimeProvider` is injected everywhere, so time-dependent logic is testable.
- **Docker:** base images are pinned by digest, the container runs as non-root, and migrations run as a separate migration-bundle container. Secrets are required through environment variables (`${VAR:?}`), and ports bind only to loopback.
- **Build:** Nullable is on, `TreatWarningsAsErrors` is set, package lock files are used with `--locked-mode`, and builds are deterministic.
- **Tests:** there are about 78 tests across unit and integration projects, plus a coverage gate.

## Where it departs from best practice

### 1. Readability (the biggest issue)
Many files put several statements on one line with no spacing. Examples:
- [JobsController.cs:17-19](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Search/JobsController.cs#L17-L19)
- [CursorCodec.cs:32](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Search/CursorCodec.cs#L32), a single ~400-character validation condition
- [JobReadStore.cs:23](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Search/JobReadStore.cs#L23)
- the `.csproj` and `appsettings.json` files, each on one line
- the tests

Other files, like [UnexpectedExceptionHandler.cs](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Diagnostics/UnexpectedExceptionHandler.cs), are formatted normally, so the style isn't even consistent. Fix: add an `.editorconfig`, run `dotnet format`, and enforce it in CI.

### 2. The search endpoint bypasses model binding
`List` reads `Request.Query` by hand through `QueryReader` instead of using a `[FromQuery]` request record. As a result:
- **The OpenAPI document shows no query parameters for `GET /api/jobs`**, so client generators and Swagger UI can't see `q`, `limit`, `sort` or `cursor`.
- **Any unknown parameter returns 400.** A cache-buster or `utm_*` tag from a frontend or proxy will break the request.
- **Error codes are vague.** Every failure becomes `invalid_query`, without saying which field was wrong.

Separately, `Detail(string id)` should use a route constraint, `{id:guid}`.

### 3. Exceptions used for control flow
`EventReader` and `QueryReader` throw `FormatException` purely to jump to a single catch block. This is an expensive and unclear way to validate, and it's why errors can't be specific. A result type, or a list of validation errors, would be cleaner. Also, `Regex.IsMatch` with an inline pattern ([EventReader.cs:67](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Contracts/EventReader.cs#L67)) should be a `[GeneratedRegex]`.

### 4. Logging is cut back too far
[Program.cs:10-24](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Program.cs#L10-L24) turns off logging entirely (`LogLevel.None`) for ASP.NET Core, EF Core, Npgsql and RabbitMQ.Client. That includes errors and critical messages, so Kestrel faults, connection-pool exhaustion and startup failures leave no trace. On top of that, every handler logs only `ex.GetType().Name`, with no message or stack trace. Hiding sensitive data is a good goal, but this goes too far. Better: set those categories to `Warning`, and log exceptions with a redaction step rather than dropping them.

### 5. Re-implementing what .NET already provides
- **Health checks:** `HealthController` and `IDatabaseProbe` duplicate `AddHealthChecks()`/`MapHealthChecks()` with tags.
- **Metrics:**
  - `SearchMetrics` uses a static `Meter` rather than `IMeterFactory`, which is the recommended approach since .NET 8.
  - The request-duration histogram duplicates the built-in `http.server.request.duration`.
  - No OpenTelemetry exporter is configured, so none of these metrics actually leave the process.
- **Request logging:** `RequestDiagnosticsMiddleware` overlaps with the built-in HTTP logging and W3C trace propagation.

### 6. Infrastructure concerns inside the controller
`JobsController` catches `NpgsqlException` itself. Mapping database exceptions to 503 belongs in an `IExceptionHandler`, which the project already has, so controllers don't depend on the Postgres driver.

### 7. Messaging trade-offs worth reconsidering
- **No limit on retries for a message that keeps failing.** A message that causes an "unexpected" (non-permanent) error tears down the session and is redelivered forever, blocking the queue. Use a quorum queue with `x-delivery-limit` plus a dead-letter queue, or count redeliveries.
- **Ingestion is effectively single-threaded.** A global advisory lock ([SearchDbContext.cs:50](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Persistence/SearchDbContext.cs#L50)) serialises every insert. This is deliberate (it keeps the snapshot watermark monotonic), but it means `Concurrency > 1` adds little. Document that limit.
- **The quarantine publisher opens a new connection and re-declares its topology for every rejected message.** That's fine for rare events but expensive during a burst of bad messages. Reuse one connection.
- **The search service consumes the producer's queue (`job-post-queue`) directly.** The docs say this is intentional, but if any other service ever subscribes to that queue, the two will split the messages between them instead of each getting a copy. The usual pattern is for each consumer to own its own queue bound to the exchange.

### 8. Smaller items
- `Program.cs` calls `SearchReads.AddSearchReads(...)` as a plain static method while the other registrations use extension syntax, and logging filters are mixed in among service registrations.
- `AppContext.SetSwitch` is called in two places, and options validation runs again inside `Configure` ([SearchPersistence.cs:12,33-35](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Persistence/SearchPersistence.cs#L12)).
- An expired cursor returns `409 Conflict`. A `400` or `410 Gone` would be more conventional.
- The RabbitMQ options default to `guest`/`guest`, and the validator doesn't reject them outside Development.
- There is no rate limiting, output caching or CORS. If a browser app calls this API directly, you'll need CORS.
- Trigram `ILIKE` can't use the index for searches shorter than 3 characters, and results have no relevance ranking. Consider PostgreSQL full-text search (`tsvector`) if ranking matters.
- The runtime Docker image installs `curl` only for the health check, which adds to the attack surface.
- `API/job-search.api/.vs/` shows as untracked; add `.vs/` to `.gitignore`.

## Verdict

| Area | Rating |
|---|---|
| Architecture and messaging reliability | Excellent |
| Data modelling and query performance | Very good |
| Security (input checks, cursors, secrets) | Very good |
| Docker and operations | Very good |
| API design and OpenAPI | Fair (manual binding hides parameters) |
| Observability | Fair (logs too silenced, metrics not exported) |

You asked for central exception handling that covers every exception. The relevant requirement is in [shared-requirements.md:39](API/job-search.api/prompt/shared-requirements.md#L39): *"Central structured safe logs and exception handling with trace IDs and ProblemDetails; suppress payloads, credentials, raw exception messages/stacks in production."*

The code only partly meets it. A central handler exists, but several code paths go around it and one isn't covered at all.

## What is covered

- **[UnexpectedExceptionHandler.cs](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Diagnostics/UnexpectedExceptionHandler.cs)** is registered with `AddExceptionHandler` and `UseExceptionHandler`. Any exception a request doesn't handle becomes a 500 ProblemDetails with a `traceId`, and only the exception type name is logged. That part is correct.
- **`AddProblemDetails` plus `UseStatusCodePages`** turn plain 404, 405 and other empty error responses into ProblemDetails.

## Where it falls short

1. **The controllers handle exceptions themselves.** `JobsController` catches database exceptions in both actions ([JobsController.cs:28](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Search/JobsController.cs#L28), [JobsController.cs:40](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Search/JobsController.cs#L40)) and turns them into 503s itself. That mapping belongs in the central pipeline, as a second `IExceptionHandler` registered before the catch-all one.

2. **Three different ProblemDetails shapes.** The controller's `Error()` has a `code` but no `type`. The central handler has a `type` but no `code`. Status-code pages produce a third format. Clients get differently shaped errors depending on which path failed. One shared factory should build all of them.

3. **The RabbitMQ consumer is outside the HTTP pipeline.** `IExceptionHandler` only sees HTTP requests. The consumer has its own catch-all in [SearchConsumerWorker.cs:19](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Messaging/SearchConsumerWorker.cs#L19), which is the right place for one, but it's a separate path that logs differently. Nothing explicitly sets what the host does if the background service fails (`BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior`).

4. **Nothing catches exceptions at the process level:**
   - **Startup failures crash the process with a raw stack trace on stderr.** An invalid cursor key, connection string or RabbitMQ setting throws an `OptionsValidationException` out of `app.Run()`. Nothing catches it, so the stack trace goes to stderr, which breaks the "no stacks in production" rule. `app.Run()` needs a try/catch that logs safely and returns a non-zero exit code.
   - **No `AppDomain.UnhandledException` or `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` handler**, so crashes on other threads and exceptions from fire-and-forget tasks are never logged.

5. **Middleware order.** `RequestDiagnosticsMiddleware` runs before `UseExceptionHandler`, so an exception thrown inside it never reaches the handler.

6. **"In production" is applied everywhere.** Details are hidden in Development too, which makes local debugging harder than the requirement asks.

**Correctly left alone:** the readiness check's catch-all in [HealthController.cs:33](API/job-search.api/src/JobSearch.Api/Diagnostics/HealthController.cs#L33) should stay. A failed probe must return 503, not a 500 error page. The parse catches in `EventReader`, `QueryReader` and `CursorCodec` are validation, not error handling.

## Suggested fix
- **A `DatabaseUnavailableExceptionHandler`** that maps database and timeout exceptions to a 503 `search_unavailable` ProblemDetails, registered before the 500 catch-all. Then remove the try/catch blocks in `JobsController`.
- **One `SearchProblems` factory** that every error path uses, so all errors include `type`, `title`, `status`, `code` and `traceId`.
- **Exception handling first in the pipeline:** move `UseExceptionHandler` ahead of the diagnostics middleware.
- **Process-level handlers:** a safe try/catch around `app.Run()`, handlers for `AppDomain.UnhandledException` and `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException`, and an explicit `BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior`.
- **Development-only detail:** include exception details in ProblemDetails and logs only when the environment is Development.
- **Tests:** update the HTTP and diagnostics tests to match, keeping the 100% coverage gate passing.
